messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Amara is a thirty-three-year-old park ranger who, fourteen months ago, lost her younger brother Kofi in the backcountry of the very park where she works. They had been hiking a remote trail she knew well—one she had patrolled for years—when a section of unstable cliff face gave way beneath his feet. She watched him fall nearly sixty feet, and by the time she rappelled down to him, he was barely conscious. He died in her arms before the search-and-rescue team could reach them, his head trauma too severe. She stayed with his body for two hours, holding him, listening to the wind.

In the months that followed, Amara found that the memory did not arrive as a story she could tell. It arrived in pieces. She would be standing at the kitchen counter and suddenly see his face in that moment—not the whole scene, just that one photograph-quality image, so clear it made her gasp. Then it would vanish, leaving her disoriented and flooded with a grief so raw it felt like the event was still happening. Other times, what surfaced was the sound of the rock breaking, or the weight of his head in her lap, each fragment as sharp and still as a photograph projected onto her mind. When these images came, the grief that followed was not a memory of sadness but the same overwhelming despair she had felt on that cliff, undiminished by time.

She had come to believe, quietly and without ever saying it aloud, that she was no longer the person who could do this job. She had always been the ranger other people called when something went wrong—steady, quick, dependable. Now she was certain that whatever had defined that version of herself was gone. When she looked in the mirror, she saw someone hollow, someone who had been permanently damaged by what she had witnessed. She told herself she felt dead inside, and the numbness frightened her more than the grief did, because at least the grief felt like something.

Amara stopped taking backcountry assignments. She told her supervisor she preferred front-country duties for a while, and she meant it—she could not imagine returning to the trail where Kofi had died. But the avoidance spread. She began to avoid the hiking trails entirely, even the easy ones on the opposite side of the park. She stopped leading the weekly guided nature walks she had once loved. She gave up her role on the search-and-rescue rotation without explanation, and her colleagues noticed. She had always been reliable; now she was the ranger who left early, who deflected questions, who sat in the visitor center with her radio turned low and her eyes fixed on the door.

At home, she had stopped relaxing. Even in the evenings, when her husband Marcus would sit down to watch television or read, Amara could not join him. Relaxing felt dangerous, as though letting her guard down invited something terrible to happen. She kept her mind occupied constantly—podcasts during her commute, music while she cooked, a running internal monologue during any quiet moment. The silence was unbearable because the silence was where the photographs appeared. At night, sleep came slowly, if it came at all. Her body stayed tense and ready, even in bed, as though the cliff were still beneath her feet and the next step could be the one that gave way.

She experienced strong negative emotions throughout her days—fear that she would never feel like herself again, anger at herself for not reaching Kofi faster, shame that she could not do her job anymore. Her body felt constantly on alert. Her shoulders stayed tight, her jaw clenched, her breathing shallow. She scanned the trails around the visitor center not with the calm attention she had once had, but with a vigilance that exhausted her. Every loose stone on the path, every uneven patch of ground, every hiker who walked too close to an edge made her pulse race.

The consequence that finally pressed her toward help was both occupational and relational. Her supervisor had gently suggested she take a desk reassignment until she was "feeling more like herself," and Amara had agreed immediately—too quickly, she now realized. She had been working the front desk for three months. She no longer felt like a park ranger. And at home, Marcus had started sleeping in the guest room because she would wake him at all hours, thrashing or crying out, and she could see in his face that he did not know how to reach her anymore. Last week, while driving home from a shift where she had done nothing but stamp entry passes, she had realized that she could not remember the last time she had felt present in her own life. That was what finally brought her to the clinic: not the memory fragments or the vigilance or the guilt, but the quiet certainty that she was watching herself disappear and did not know how to stop it. She said she wanted to feel like herself again, but she was afraid she had already changed too much to ever go back.
